content: Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) has long been the primary conservative treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Weighted vaginal cones are an alternative method designed to assist women in strengthening their pelvic floor muscles. These cones are inserted into the vagina, and the pelvic floor muscles are contracted to prevent the cones from slipping out. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of vaginal cones in managing female stress urinary incontinence. Specifically, the review aimed to compare the following: (1) vaginal cones versus no treatment, (2) vaginal cones versus other conservative therapies such as PFMT or electrostimulation, (3) a combination of vaginal cones and another conservative therapy versus either therapy alone, and (4) vaginal cones versus non-conservative methods like surgery or injectable treatments. Secondary considerations included whether vaginal cones are quicker to teach compared to PFMT, whether self-taught use of cones is effective, whether the ability to retain heavier cones correlates with improvement, and whether certain subgroups of women benefit more from cone use. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Trials Register, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to March 2013. They also reviewed reference lists of relevant articles. The inclusion criteria were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing weighted vaginal cones with other treatments or no treatment. Two reviewers independently assessed the studies for inclusion and quality, and data were extracted and cross-checked. Study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. The review included 23 trials involving 1,806 women, of whom 717 were treated with vaginal cones. Most of the trials were small, and the quality of the studies was often difficult to assess. The outcome measures varied significantly between trials, making it challenging to combine results. High dropout rates were reported in several studies for both cone and comparison treatments. Seven of the trials were only available as abstracts. The findings indicated that vaginal cones were more effective than no active treatment in managing SUI (rate ratio [RR] for failure to cure incontinence: 0.84, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.76 to 0.94). However, there was little evidence of a difference in subjective cure rates between vaginal cones and PFMT (RR: 1.01, 95% CI: 0.91 to 1.13) or between vaginal cones and electrostimulation (RR: 1.26, 95% CI: 0.85 to 1.87), though the confidence intervals were wide. There was insufficient evidence to determine whether combining vaginal cones with PFMT was more effective than either treatment alone. Only seven trials assessed quality of life, and none evaluated economic outcomes. Seven trials included women with symptoms of incontinence, while others required women to have urodynamic stress incontinence, except for one trial with unclear inclusion criteria. The authors concluded that there is some evidence suggesting that weighted vaginal cones are more effective than no treatment for women with SUI and may be as effective as PFMT or electrostimulation. However, this conclusion is tentative due to the small size and variable quality of the trials. Larger, high-quality studies with standardized and relevant outcome measures are needed. Vaginal cones could be considered as a treatment option for SUI, provided that women find them acceptable.
